rewrites.title: Timed degron depletion to separate maintenance from encoding
rewrites.description: Acutely degrade AP-1 (dTAG or auxin degron on JUN/FOS) at different times after priming: during induction, during a quiescent interval, and at late timepoints. If AP-1 is required only for encoding, degradation after the interval should not erase the memory; if AP-1 is continuously required for maintenance, the primed response will be lost. The readout is target-gene reinduction on re-stimulation.

rewrites.title: Separating AP-1 protein persistence from mitotic chromatin bookmarking
rewrites.description: Combine cycloheximide or other protein-synthesis blockers, and a light-inducible AP-1 nuclear export switch, with the re-stimulation assay to test whether memory needs ongoing AP-1 protein or only the chromatin state it left behind. Mitotic chromatin retention assays, such as live imaging of AP-1 on mitotic chromosomes, test whether AP-1 stays bound to its sites through division.

rewrites.title: Washout time-course with inducible AP-1 degradation
rewrites.description: Test whether an AP-1-dependent transcriptional state outlasts the stimulus. Pulse cells with a defined stimulus, wash it out, and use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to remove c-Fos or c-Jun at different times. Track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and target-gene expression over days. If the state persists after AP-1 protein is gone, AP-1 triggers a self-sustaining state rather than being the memory itself.

rewrites.title: Lineage-stable reporter of cell-state memory across divisions
rewrites.description: Combine an activity-dependent Fos reporter or FosTRAP-style recorder with single-cell lineage barcoding, and follow the marked cells through several divisions and days after stimulus. If AP-1 maintains a memory, reporter-positive lineages should keep a primed transcriptional state and faster response even when AP-1 protein has returned to baseline.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 depletion during the inter-stimulus interval
rewrites.description: Prime cells with one stimulus, then use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Fos or Jun to remove AP-1 during the rest period before a second stimulus. Memory is defined as faster or stronger re-induction; if the primed advantage disappears only when AP-1 is degraded during the gap, AP-1 is required to store the memory and not just to read it out.

rewrites.title: Lineage tracing and cell-division persistence
rewrites.description: Mark primed cells (e.g., with a FOS-driven Cre or reporter) and follow their progeny through divisions in vivo or in organoids. Measure whether accessibility, AP-1 occupancy, and enhanced responses are inherited over generations and whether they are lost on a predicted schedule. Pair with live-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters to distinguish a self-sustaining feedback loop (e.g., FOS/JUN autoregulation) from a chromatin-based memory.

rewrites.title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracking of AP-1 history
rewrites.description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC with a fluorescent AP-1 reporter or barcoded lineage tracing to link past AP-1 activity to current chromatin state across cell divisions. Test whether daughter cells inherit the accessibility and responsiveness of mother cells and whether inheritance depends on AP-1 dosage, quantifying heritability versus noise.

rewrites.title: Priming and re-stimulation challenge
rewrites.description: Compare naive cells with previously stimulated cells in a second challenge, measuring the speed and amplitude of transcription (nascent RNA, live reporters) at AP-1 targets. Hypersensitive responses specific to AP-1 sites that disappear when AP-1 is blocked only during priming would indicate AP-1-dependent memory.

rewrites.title: Transient stimulus with AP-1 chromatin tracking
rewrites.description: Give cells a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then measure after the stimulus is gone whether AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, accessibility (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN), and primed target-gene responses persist for days to weeks. Compare naive and pre-exposed cells on re-stimulation to quantify faster or stronger transcription, the hallmark of memory.

rewrites.title: Stimulus washout and persistence time course
rewrites.description: Give a brief AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF pulse, or a doxycycline-inducible FOS/JUN pulse), then withdraw it and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription over days. Memory requires that AP-1 target enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself has returned to baseline, so persistence beyond the signal is the key readout.

rewrites.title: AP-1 mitotic bookmarking and inheritance of potentiated re-induction
rewrites.description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN/ATF in live mitotic cells (plus mitotic CUT&RUN and H3S10ph-matched controls) to quantify retention on condensed chromatin at specific enhancers. Also stimulate mother cells, track single daughter cells by lineage imaging, and test whether potentiated re-induction is inherited and whether it is lost when bookmarking is disrupted by an AP-1 DNA-binding-deficient or mitosis-evicted mutant.

rewrites.title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
rewrites.description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC with live reporters of AP-1 activity, and track cells across divisions by barcodes or time-lapse imaging. Test whether primed accessibility and responsiveness pass from mother to daughter cells and whether they decay in a heritable, cell-autonomous way rather than reflecting continuing signaling.

rewrites.title: Genomic recorder of past AP-1 activity
rewrites.description: Engineer an AP-1-responsive enhancer driving a recombinase or base editor that writes a permanent DNA barcode when AP-1 is active, then read the written mark jointly with scRNA-seq or ATAC days later. This tests, cell by cell, whether a past AP-1 episode predicts present transcriptional and chromatin state independently of current AP-1 levels.

rewrites.title: Mitotic bookmarking test of AP-1-marked enhancers
rewrites.description: After priming, sort or image cells in mitosis and measure whether AP-1 and its associated enhancer marks remain on DNA through mitosis (live imaging of tagged JUN, mitotic ChIP-seq). Then check whether daughter cells re-activate target genes faster on the same stimulus. Retention through division is a strong criterion for stable cellular memory, and loss of bookmarking with preserved memory would argue against AP-1 being the carrier.

rewrites.title: Prime–rest–restimulate recall assay with motif-dependent enhancers
rewrites.description: Measure faster or stronger re-induction by RNA-seq/PRO-seq after a second stimulus following a rest period, and link genes showing memory to AP-1 motif content. Validate with CRISPR deletion or base-editing of AP-1 motifs at specific memory enhancers, plus reporter assays, to show the motif is necessary for the primed response.

rewrites.title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
rewrites.description: Expose cells to a brief pulse of a stimulus (e.g., serum, TNF, or injury) that activates AP-1 (FOS/JUN), wash it out, and profile accessibility and AP-1 binding by ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN at days to weeks. Persistence of open regions containing AP-1 motifs after the stimulus is gone would show a lasting memory footprint. Naive and pulsed cells provide the baseline comparison.

rewrites.title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
rewrites.description: Use auxin/dTAG degron alleles of FOS/JUN family members (or a dominant-negative A-Fos) before, during, and long after the priming stimulus. If AP-1 is needed only at priming but not at recall, it is an initiator; if depletion during the memory phase erases enhanced re-induction, AP-1 is the maintenance mechanism.

rewrites.title: Degron depletion to separate establishment from maintenance
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous FOS, JUN, and JUNB with dTAG/AID degrons and acutely deplete them either during the initial stimulus or only during the post-stimulus memory window. Persistence of memory after later depletion implies AP-1 writes a chromatin mark it no longer needs to hold, whereas loss of memory implies continuous AP-1 occupancy is itself the memory.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
rewrites.description: Use an inducible degron tag on c-Jun or c-Fos to remove AP-1 at different stages: during the initial stimulus, during the washout interval, or just before re-stimulation. Then determine which stage is needed for the memory signature (chromatin marks, transcriptional priming, and altered response). This shows whether AP-1 is required to maintain the memory or only to establish it, i.e., whether the factor must stay bound to keep the state.

rewrites.title: Timed degron removal to map the window of AP-1 dependence
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN/JUNB with dTAG or AID degrons and degrade AP-1 at a graded series of delays after a priming pulse, then assay survival of the primed enhancer landscape and the potentiated secondary response. The delay at which degradation no longer erases memory defines the handoff from AP-1 to a maintenance mechanism such as nucleosome positioning, a partner transcription factor, or DNA methylation loss.
